proof.claim:
Two machines must never both hold the same node identity.

THE FAULT. Copy one node's entire persisted state onto another node's volume,
then start it. Two containers now present the same node_id, the same keys and
the same certificates, each with a complete and internally consistent claim.

    node-4 state  ──copy──▶  node-5 volume
          ↓
    node-5 starts, presenting node-4's identity

WHY THIS IS REACHABLE IN PRACTICE. This is not an exotic attack; it is what
restoring a backup onto replacement hardware does, and what cloning a VM does.
It is also what happens when a node is rebuilt from a snapshot taken before it
was decommissioned. No packet is dropped and no process crashes — the fault is
purely that two actors hold identical evidence of being the same node.

WHY EXISTING SCENARIOS CANNOT REACH IT. Every node-level scenario in the suite
moves one node between up and down. None creates a second claimant. Identity
collision is invisible to availability testing because nothing is unavailable.

WHAT MUST HOLD. The cluster must not end up with two members sharing one
identity: either the impostor is refused before it can register, or it is
admitted only as a distinct identity. What is forbidden is a cluster that
accepts both and then quietly interleaves their heartbeats, installed-state
writes and runtime proofs under one node_id — because from then on every
per-node record has two writers and no way to tell them apart.

This scenario is destructive and its cleanup is deliberately thorough: it wipes
the impostor's state and removes any duplicate record so the cluster is left
with exactly the identities it started with.
